en: Vaiśampāyana said: Having praised the one whose body bears the Śrīvatsa mark, the world-honored Śāṇḍilya was questioned by the sages rich in asceticism who had performed great penance.
O Blessed One, we wish to hear about the nature of the worship and the ritual acts of Viṣṇu, whose deeds are marvelous; please describe them according to their essential character.
Śāṇḍilya said: Listen all of you with self-restraint; this scripture, which is the very essence, was indeed spoken by Viṣṇu himself, who possesses immeasurable splendor. 3.
By the powerful Viṣṇu, while residing at Badarikāśrama,
[this was told] to the sages who had been liberated by the gods, as well as to Nārada and Nara.
O best of sages, listen to that knowledge which delivers one from the cycle of worldly existence, [revealed] by Tārkṣya, Mṛkaṇḍa, and the most exalted Ādityas. 5.
In response to what was asked by Nārada, he related the beneficial account of the victory,
and how penance was performed for the sake of joy during the battle with Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Furthermore, that form which is endowed with power for the sake of victory was indeed described by him to the inquiring Nārada from the north.
Therefore, this is the essential point here: it is established that victory is supreme.
All this excellent knowledge from of old has been heard by me from Nārada. (8)
The entire world was created by you and sustained by you, O Lord;
and it is held together by you through the power of yoga, O God Keśava.
O Lord of Gods, tell me truly that mantra and that yoga, by which I may know that Brahma, the Lord of the Lords of Yoga. 10.

O All-pervading Lord, may I and Your devotees always perform the recitation of mantras, sacrifice, worship, meditation, and yoga that bestows liberation, as well as knowledge and the object of knowledge. || 11 ||
The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, Nārada! You have asked me about this essence.
For all that I have been questioned by you is preceded by mantra."
Therefore, I shall proclaim the auspicious mantra that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On a level, pure plot of ground smeared with cow-dung, the practitioner of mantras, having performed worship, should spread out the *mātṛkā* and extract [the letters]. || 13 ||
One should write out the eight groups according to the division of the classes of vowels;
the seed-syllable at the beginning of each group is that which ends the group, distinguished by the seven groups in pairs. 14.
Endowed with five dots at its head and conjoined with Vyomeśa, this divine and excellent seed-syllable bestows the fruit of all desires. 15.
The third letter from Ananteśa, joined with the final letter of the vowel group, and its second [consonant]—that is its seed-syllable, which removes the fear of old age and death. 16.
The first of the vowels and the fifth [consonant] are joined in the twenty-fifth [position].
One should write the seed-syllable (bīja) of those two, which is the first, auspicious, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 17.
These three seeds are my supreme body, the syllable of Yoga;
they take the form of the moon, the sun, and fire, and constitute the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
The support of all worlds without exception, the bestower of sovereignty over the three realms,
the substratum of the powers such as *aṇimā*, and the one who raises up practitioners from the netherworld.
One should meditate upon the four-armed God, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace;
who has four faces, beautiful eyes, a lovely countenance, and a lotus in his hand.
Vaikuṇṭha, Nārasiṃha, Vārāha, and Kapilānana;
Śukla, mounted upon the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) and adorned with all ornaments. 21.
The Lord, endowed with all auspicious marks, wearing garlands and fine garments,
the beginningless and endless God, the sovereign creator of the universe.
It bestows liberation upon one who desires liberation; it grants wealth to one who desires wealth;
it grants a kingdom to one who desires sovereignty; and it grants enjoyments to one who desires enjoyment.
Whatever desire the practitioner prays for, that very thing it bestows.

Lakṣmī, Kīrti, Jayā, and Māyā—these goddesses reside as his attendants; they should be meditated upon by the preeminent practitioner for the sake of his own accomplishment, as well as for [the attainment of] his wife. (24)
Some had one eye and others two eyes; they were two-armed, adorned with beautiful earrings, lovely like lotus petals, and decorated with girdles and strings of beads.
Wearing white garlands and garments, adorned with necklaces and armlets,
they were endowed with all auspicious marks and possessed full, elevated breasts.
The goddesses, holding nooses and goads, are the accomplishers of all desires and goals;
they sit in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana) facing the God of gods. || 27 ||

I shall proclaim the supreme heart-mantra for their worship, which is the second [mantra] following the root mantra; it is the Lord who is the sovereign of the seed-syllables. Indeed, this is proclaimed as the common heart-mantra for all of them. 28.
I shall describe, according to the truth, the limbs of the God of gods,
by means of which the prepared practitioner becomes invulnerable even to the thirty deities.
But that seed-syllable which is preceded by the letter 'a', joined with the heart (ha) and the bindu, and conjoined with the second vowel—that very same one one should place upon the head. || 30 ||
(4) That which is joined with the vowel *s* (*śi*) is proclaimed as the *śikhā*; that which is joined with the five vowels is designated as the *kavaca*. 31.
This eye is proclaimed as being joined with the vowel *au*;
that same [syllable] with the *visarga* is the weapon. One should apply that [weapon] to the letter *ha*.
These limbs of the God one should always join within oneself. 32.
One should likewise fashion the mantra for the Ocean of Milk (*kṣīroda*) as ending with "namas," preceded by "dīrgha" and joined with "amṛtam" situated within "varuṇa. (33)
One should fashion the support together with a lotus, ending with the word "namas";
this is prescribed for the seat of the God of Gods at the time of worship. 34.
And I shall proclaim the mantra of Khageśa, which grants the accomplishment of all aims;
one should fashion it beginning with the Praṇava and ending with "namas" to Khageśa. (35)
Thus ends the first chapter, the Extraction of Mantras, in the Jayottara.
The Blessed One said:
I shall proclaim the treasury of mudrās, in which Hari is ever present;
it shall indeed bring about the attainment of enjoyment and liberation for practitioners. 1.
O Sage, first for the God of gods, and thereafter for others, one should cause [the disciple] to grasp the middle finger with the left hand turned downwards. || 2 ||
Having placed the little finger of the right hand and the other three fingers together like a fist,
and raising the thumb, this is known as the Jayā mudrā.
Below that, one should contemplate Garuḍa in the left hand;
on his back, in the right hand, one should meditate upon the eternal Viṣṇu.
This mudrā, named Jayā, accomplishes all purposes and goals;
one should employ it for the God of gods together with Khageśa. 5.
One should place the fingers of the left hand over those of the right;
then, one should join the tips of the left index finger with the two thumbs.
This is the mudrā of Śaṅkha;
it is positioned with the palms facing upward, the two thumbs joined together, and the fingers remaining spread apart.
This shall be the mudrā of Padma; one will obtain nourishment and good fortune.
The two hands are clearly extended and joined with one another. 8.
From its rotation, it is proclaimed as the Cakravartin-mudrā;
it is the destroyer of all wicked ones, and the Tarjanī is the supreme among mudrās. 9.
The fist is bound with the right hand upon the top of the left thumb;
this beautiful mudrā of the right hand is indeed that of Kaumodakī, renowned as the Gada-mudrā, which crushes the armies of enemies. 9.

The practitioner of mantras should employ the mantra, beginning with Oṃ and ending with Svāhā, for the Śaṅkha and the others up to the Gadā, for the complete liberation of those who are bound. || 10 ||
Thus ends the second chapter, on Mudrās, in the Jayottara.
The Blessed One said:
I shall now explain the application of ritual procedures, the yoga of placement (nyāsa), the practice of recitation (japa), and so forth.
One should perform the two kinds of bathing for the sake of purifying any suspicion of impurity. (1)
Having bathed according to the general rule, one should then perform the specific rite;
the general bath is the worldly one, while the specific is that consecrated by the Mantras. || 2 ||
Three applications of clay should be made to the penis with intervals between each;
five should be applied to the left hand, and three to both hands for the sake of purification.
The purification after voiding urine and immediately after voiding feces is as follows:
there should be five applications of clay to the anus, with three applications of clay between each.
Ten [handfuls] should be given with the left hand; seven for both hands together;
purification of the feet is prescribed with three, or of the waist with seven.
Likewise, purification should be performed according to the place and time;
it is well-determined that during the rainy season, the cleansing of the shanks should be done with five [handfuls]. 6.
Three [days] in summer and one more in the cold season are thus proclaimed;
by removing all traces of perfume and ointment, one becomes pure through the purification of the mind.
Having bathed, one should assign the mantras and perform the binding of the mudrās;
having first performed the bath for removing impurities, one should carry out the ritual bath according to the rules.

Having taken earth consecrated with the Astra-mantra, one should scatter it in the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, below, and above the sacred bathing place; then one should touch the limbs of one's own body.

While muttering the Astra mantra, one should bathe for the purification of impurities and sins; having turned the face slightly to the left, one should perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules.
Having taken clay mixed with water, one should first utter the Astra-mantra;
then, one should divide it threefold upon the left hand, according to the root, middle, and tip [of the fingers]. || 11 ||
One should recite the root mantra along with the ancillary mantras in their proper sequence;
then, taking the earth consecrated by the weapon-mantra, one should scatter it in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Then, both below and above the sacred site (tīrtha), one should apply the clay body to the root-tīrtha while joined with the binding of mudrās and the limb-mantras (aṅgamantras). || 13 ||
Having cast [the water] in all directions, one should contemplate the Cakratīrtha as being filled with the waters of the Gaṅgā and the auspicious waters of the Yamunā.
Having meditated there upon Prayāga, one should then contemplate the Puṣkara lakes;
having bound the sacred site (tīrtha) by that very means, one should perform the ritual bath while reciting the mantra. 15.
Then, one should satisfy all the ancestors and the gods with the syllable Om (praṇava);
the dismissal of the sacred site (tīrtha) should be performed with the root mantra.
Having bathed and applied unguents, one should then perform worship with perfumes and garlands;
having touched one's own body, one should then deploy the mantras.
Thus ends the third chapter, on bathing, in the Jayottara.
The Blessed One said:
Now, one who possesses the mantra should perform the ritual of worship preceded by the ritual of placement (nyāsa), beginning with his own seat, which consists of the ocean together with a lotus. 1.
Then, having meditated upon the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) with special offerings,
one should clear the directions with the Astra-mantra and veil them with the Kavaca-mantra.
Then, having performed the purification of the hands, one should again perform the placement upon the body (dehanyāsa):
the root mantra on the thumb, and the deities on the index finger and the others.
Having placed the four [syllables] ending with the little finger, one should then assign the limbs (aṅgas),
beginning with the heart, in due order to those ending with the little finger.
One should then apply the Astra-mantra from the big toe up to the tips of the fingernails, and the Locana-mantra;
thereafter, one should place the Lord Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa within the body.
Having first applied the root mantra, one should then apply the deities;
one should place Lakṣmī on the left shoulder and Kīrti on the right.
One should join Jayā, who is stationed in the right hand, with Māyā in the left;
then, one should place the limbs, beginning with the heart, in their respective locations in due order.
Then, having formed the mudrā, one should meditate upon oneself in the form of Viṣṇu—
either in one's own form, or as the universal form (viśvarūpa), or in whatever form is desired.
Then one should employ the mudrās, such as the conch and others, together with their respective mantras.
Having meditated upon the Ocean of Milk at the navel, one should then visualize a lotus arisen therefrom.
Upon its back, one should place the Lord of the Kings of Birds, consisting of ego (ahaṃkāra);
and [one should place] the Intellect (buddhi), which has the qualities as its primary substance, with the Lord established presiding over it. 10.
[He saw] the god Viṣṇu, the soul of the universe, whose body is the support of the Lord (Īśvara), standing above the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) in the sky, his form adorned [with ornaments]. 11.
Then one should meditate on the body of the mantra according to its gross and subtle divisions;
thereafter, one should meditate upon it as consisting of light, and then again as consisting of sound.
The Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa is even a hundred-thousandth part of the tip of a hair;
he is the enjoyer of the guṇas, the substratum of the guṇas, possessed of guṇas, and yet devoid of guṇas. 13.
The Lord of the body is renowned as the sovereign who consists of all the gods;
the Person, the size of a thumb, dwells within all bodies. 14.
Just as a gem, though possessed of distinctions such as yellow, blue, and so forth,
undergoes a change in its appearance, so too does the all-pervading Lord undergo a change in His state of meditation.
Whether it be Brahmā, or Rudra, Soma, Sūrya, or Prajāpati—
all these are known to have originated from the Supreme Self and are therefore of its very nature.
Those deities, Lakṣmī and the others, are the embodiments of dispassion and sovereignty;
therefore, He, together with His limbs (aṅgas), should be worshipped within the lotus of the heart.
Intent on meditation in his mind with offerings of perfumes, garlands, and the like,
he should then worship the God externally upon a ground site possessing auspicious characteristics.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Chapter on Nyāsa, in the Jayottara.
The Blessed One said:
Now, having performed the purification of the ground, I shall explain in brief the arrangement of the mandala of Viṣṇu, who possesses immeasurable splendor. 1.
Having examined the earth in various ways—free from wicked thorns, auspicious, capable of bearing a burden, firm, and endowed with excellent fragrance and color. || 2 ||
Behind that, one should construct a mandala adorned with white plaster,
well-decorated with canopies, banners, and cloths.
At the beginning, one should diligently mark the center as the Brahma-sthāna;
having reached the Brahma-sthāna, one should draw a very beautiful lotus.
One should worship the wheel with sixteen spokes using the sixteen vowels,
or the one with twelve spokes joined with the twelve syllables.
Or one should always draw an eight-spoked [wheel], complete with a hub and a rim;
the straight spokes, beautifully adorned, are indeed pervaded by the eight groups of consonants.
Upon the nave of the wheel, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with a pericarp,
adorned with filaments, clearly delineated, and beautified with four colors.
One should make the pericarp yellow in color, the beautiful filaments yellowish-red,
the eight petals white, and the intermediate space like the sky.
Alternatively, one should draw a very beautiful lotus inside a conch shell, or on the hilt of the Kaumodakī mace,
or on the back of the Nandaka sword.
Or it may be fashioned as a garland of flowers; or, O Sage, for the attainment of one's desires, a lotus should be made in the center, or else a lotus [should be drawn]. || 10 ||
There is a set of four lotuses in the cardinal directions for the worship of the goddesses,
and four others in the intermediate directions where Satyā and the other [goddesses] reside.
Among them, the ninth is worshipped where Keśava resides;
there the Lord is to be worshipped both with his limbs and as the partless (niṣkala).
This sacrifice within the interior of the lotus is proclaimed as the "all-encompassing sacrifice" (sarvayāga).
[It is performed] from the front of the lotuses of the directions toward the doors in the four cardinal quarters.
In the case of the "joined nine-petalled lotus," one should make a pathway with half the measure of the interior;
thus is the sacrifice performed within the lotus-bud. Now hear about the other [sacrifice] within the pot-belly.
The jar should be made of gold, silver, copper, or firm clay;
it must be free from kālamūla insects and devoid of cracks or holes. || 15 ||
Then, having filled it with milk— or else with curds or fragrant water—
it should be thickly infused with all kinds of gems and medicinal herbs, and its interior should contain sprouts of kuśa and dūrvā grass.
It was anointed with sandalwood paste marked by conch shells, svastikas, and lotuses;
it was beautified with white garments, silk cloths, garlands, and other ornaments. || 17 ||
In the center of that, one should meditate upon a lotus, and in the center of that, Janārdana, seated upon Vainateya; Lakṣmī and the others are situated in the cardinal directions.
Having placed the limbs in the intermediate directions and the weapons outside of them,
one should worship with these excellent offerings that which grants all desires.

With various kinds of foods to be chewed, eaten, licked, swallowed, and sucked, as well as with offerings of honey-mixture (madhuparka), portions of food, and diverse types of milk-rice (pāyasa). || 20 ||
Having thus satisfied the Lord of Gods, whether in a water-pot or even in a mandala, || 21 ||
When one satisfies the God by means of the prescribed rite of recitation (japayajña),
then He grants whatever desired object for all one's wishes, even as wished for in the mind.
One should perform the threefold recitation while holding the rosary in one's hand:
the vocal recitation for minor rites, and the whispered recitation for rites of accomplishment.
For the sake of the practice leading to liberation, one should always meditate upon the God with a focused mind;
a beautiful rosary should be worn, invisible to other people. 24.
One should fashion the beads so that they are the size of a dice-bone when completed;
the measurement of the interior of a dhātrī fruit is considered the medium size. 25.
The smallest [vessel] is declared to be the size of a jujube fruit;
it should contain one hundred and eight [grains], or half of that, or even a quarter.
One should perform that which is prescribed by the ritual rules, impelled by the injunctions of one's own specific rite;
for the sake of accomplishing material success, one should have an excellent golden [image] fashioned there. (27)
Silver is for rites for the ancestors and for the sake of obtaining beauty;
copper is for the sake of obtaining splendor; and iron is for minor tasks.
One who desires prosperity should begin the recitation using beads made of tin or lead for Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas, as well as lotus seeds and conch shells.
A coral bead should be worn for good fortune; a pearl for all accomplishments;
beads made of putrajīva fruit for the sake of liberation; and a crystal for rites of pacification.
Having performed the sacrifice in two ways, one should commence the rite of recitation;
when the sacrifice is performed within the interior of a lotus, Lakṣmī is always pleased. 31.

Through the Nandaka sword one gains a kingdom; through the mace, one becomes fortunate; through the conch, one achieves rites of pacification; and through the flower-mandala, there is indeed nourishment.
Within the center of the wheel, there shall be sovereignty that causes the destruction of the enemy faction;
on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), however, one should perform what is auspicious, which bestows all auspicious accomplishments (siddhis). 33.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Maṇḍalapaṭala, in the Jayottara.
The Blessed One said:
Then, with devotion, one should satisfy the omnipresent Lord situated within the fire with sesame seeds, ghee, and milk, O lotus-colored and most beautiful lady. 1.
With fuel-sticks produced from the Brahma-tree (palāśa) as well as from milky trees,
with stalks of white dūrvā grass, white flowers, milk-rice, or barley.
With guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter, as well as auspicious blue lotuses;
with amṛtā plants combined with milk, and udumbara wood pieces soaked in honey. || 3 ||
For they have uncut tips, are not broken, and are free from thorns;
all of them are provided with the three sweets, or alternatively, mixed with ghee.
With lotuses and bilva fruits smeared with clarified butter, Lakṣmī quickly bestows her fruit;
one desiring subjugation should use blue lotuses, and one desiring enjoyment should use guggulu resin.
Through the oblation of dūrvā grass, amṛtā, and other such substances, one shall obtain an increase in longevity;
an oblation with auspicious fuel-sticks (samidh), however, bestows the fruit of all-pacifying rites.
On an auspicious day, under a favorable constellation,
during the bright fortnight and on the twelfth lunar day, the Lord, abiding in the fire, accomplishes virtue, desire, and wealth.
Good fortune is attained on the thirteenth day, certain victory on the eleventh;
for the sake of success in wealth on the fifth, and for being dear to the deities on the ninth.
The lunar days (tithis) in the bright fortnight are prescribed for rites concerning prosperity;
however, one who seeks liberation may perform them according to his desire during both fortnights.

They know that for rites performed for specific desires, the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions, being either square, equal, or circular and pleasing to the mind.
For the daily and occasional fire-oblations (homa), the hearth should be either circular or square;
it should be provided with three tiers (mekhalā) and equipped with both a rim (oṣṭha) and a navel (nābhi).
One should make the pedestal square in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
one should fashion a lotus in the center, situated within the lotus, which bestows prosperity.
One should scrape [the ground] with the king of weapons, sprinkle it with the armor-mantra, strike it with the weapon-mantra, and then extract [the deity] with the heart-mantra. || 13 ||
One should sprinkle it with the armor-mantra (kavaca), crush it immediately thereafter, smear it with fragrant water, and worship it with white flowers. || 14 ||
In the secret garden of trees, at the arrangement of the crossroads, and during the worship of the three girdles, one should employ the heart-mantra. || 15 ||
Then, with the syllable Om (praṇava), one should worship the navel, which resembles the moon;
having worshipped the three principles (tattva) situated within the triple girdle.
With the syllable Om, one should worship the fire situated at the navel, which consists of the nature of Agni and Soma;
having meditated upon it, one should cast that fire out from one's own body by means of that path. 17.
Joined with the word *dūtī* and awakened by *bindu* and *nāda*, one should cast it into the fire by means of the end of *nāda*; thus one should purify the fire within the fire.
Holding it with both hands and whirling it, one should cast it into the vessel;
having been consecrated by the five purificatory rites, it is placed upon the path of the womb with the Gāyatrī mantra.
One should ensure that his embryo remains stable and perform the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras),
well-prepared through these rites up to the final one, the naming ceremony.
One should perform the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) using the Heart-mantra with moistened hands;
then the strewing (staraṇa) with the Astra-mantra, and the laying of the enclosing sticks (paridhi) with the Heart-mantra.
Then one should always offer seats upon their backs with the Hṛdaya-mantra;
thereafter, one should constantly worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) situated in their respective directions. || 22 ||
One should perform the consecration of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Rudra with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
as well as the purification of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with *kuśa* grass blades that have upward-pointing tips and are placed within the *upayāma*.
The *sruva* ladle is to be purified twelve times, and the *sruc* ladles likewise twice;
furthermore, there are ten purificatory rites for the fire situated within the sacrificial pit.
Externally, however, there are five purificatory rites; thus fifteen are traditionally taught:
sprinkling, striking, worship, and veiling.

The immortalization [of the fire], the worship with the Gāyatrī mantra, the placement of the embryo (garbhanyāsa), the rite for male progeny (puṃsavana), and likewise the fashioning of the faces. || 26 ||
The parting of the hair, the emergence from the mouth, the birth-rite,
the naming ceremony, and likewise all the purificatory rites should indeed be performed with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
The triad beginning with Prabhā is situated in the southeast, south, and southwest;
likewise, the triad beginning with Marīci is in the northwest, north, and northeast.
In the center, between the Vāruṇa and Māhendra [fires], stands that one called Lelihānā;
she indeed performs the rites with clarified butter according to the tenfold rule. || 29 ||

The acts beginning with placing [the vessel] on the fire are performed with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, while leaping up, plunging down, and placing [the vessel] on the fire are performed with the *kavaca-mantra*.
The placing upon the support, as well as the purification, should be performed with the Heart-mantra;
the veiling, however, should be done with the Armor-mantra.
Having gazed [at them] and made them immortal, the two eyes should indeed be given;
by means of that clarified butter, all the consecratory rites, including the oblations, are to be performed with sesame and boiled rice.
In all purificatory rites, an oblation must be offered into the fire;
then, having performed worship according to one's ability to that consecrated fire. 33.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to one's capacity, following the sequence of sesame seeds, clarified butter, and so forth;
one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) into the fire with clarified butter, ending with the syllable "vauṣaṭ."
Then, worship should be performed for the God in the midst of the fire;
having meditated upon the fire as being like the sky, one should worship the Lord in its center. 35.
Then, with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should worship the Astra-kalasha (the vessel of the weapon-mantra) on the right arm-path near the fire-pit.
Having worshipped the deity who consists of Agni and Soma for the sake of self-protection, as well as the discus, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa).
Having worshipped with sesame seeds, clarified butter, and all sacrificial materials,
he should then perform everything according to the prescribed rule, beginning with the clarified butter and other offerings.
One should perform the oblation with one karṣa of clarified butter and especially of milk;
the offering of curd is the measure of a śukti, while that of milk-rice is a prasṛti.
One should take half a mouthful of solid food according to one's own capacity,
and three pieces of roots or fruits according to their own size.
One should offer five handfuls of fine parched grains;
pills the size of a jujube fruit made from guggulu resin should always be offered as oblations. 41.
One should cause kṛsarā to be offered in a quantity equal to the fruit of the dhātrī; the offering of sesame seeds is always recommended when performed with the śaṅkha mudrā. 42.
The practitioner should always offer as an oblation a handful of each type of grain,
and a portion the size of a pearl-shell of milk-rice mixed with sesame seeds.
The sacrificial fuel sticks should be the size of a span (prādeśa) and be accompanied by their bark;
one should always utter "svāhā" during the oblation, and "vauṣaṭ" during the full oblation.
One should employ "suvaṣaṭ" in rites for pacification (śāntika), while "vaṣaṭ" is beneficial for rites of nourishment (āpyāyana).
The word *svadhā* is used in rites for the ancestors, while *phaṭ* is used in rites of destruction.
For the rite of incantation, "huṃ" is used for causing enmity and "hrīṃ" for subjugation;
likewise, for the sake of accomplishing the ritual action, one should offer oblations into a fire fueled by many sacrificial offerings.
One should know that for the accomplishment of rites, the colors, scents, sounds, and forms of the fire, as well as its flames, must remain free from any alteration.
O Sage, for the sake of victory over the fire, a gem of excellent quality is praised that has the luster of a ruby, or one resembling lac-dye, or the color of the rising sun. 48.
A fire resembling an indragopaka insect, or one that is beautiful,
or resembling Indra’s bow (the rainbow), as well as one with the appearance of saffron, is praised.
In this context, fire is intended by the color of red varieties of flowers.
The fragrance of fragrant substances and the smell of ghee from the fire are auspicious. || 50 ||
For long life, there should be the scent of lotus and the scent of bilva, O observer of good vows;
however, for malevolent rites (abhicāra), a fierce scent is always prescribed, as is that of fire.
The sound of fire that resounds with the tones of clouds, lutes, conchs, and mṛdaṅga drums is a cause of success; any other sound would be a source of failure.
The best [mark] for Bhṛgu is the shape of an umbrella, as are those of a banner, a chowrie, a pavilion, a canopy, a temple, or a bull. (53)
Furthermore, by the appearance of swans or peacocks, success is granted; likewise,
when the flame is glossy, turning clockwise, and its sound is muffled by the wind,
one should offer oblations into that blazing, licking fire for the accomplishment of one's rites.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, on the fire-ritual, in the Jayottara.
The Blessed One said:
Now I shall explain the initiation for disciples who are seekers, by means of which they may attain the authority to perform worship of the gods, the fire, and the guru. (1)
For the sake of both spiritual accomplishment and liberation, I shall describe that [practice] in three ways;
it should be performed by men of limited means according to their capacity.
One should have it performed by those wealthy in means through the yoga of the great maṇḍala, provided that the embodied being has abandoned greed for wealth and possesses a peaceful mind. (3)
One who is terrified by the fear of saṃsāra and is a devotee of Viṣṇu should have [this] performed;
having fully understood the reality of Viṣṇu, he should bestow grace upon all. 4.
Having correctly understood the threefold reality of Viṣṇu, the preceptor, the teacher,
may bestow grace through mere words upon one who is destitute of material offerings.
Having examined those who are endowed with devotion, always established in celibacy,
and observant of restraints, he should cause them to fast for one night.
Then, having given the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for the purification of those who have eaten improperly— once they have bathed well, put on clean garments, and purified their bodies—
one should, according to the prescribed rite, fashion for them a body consisting of mantras.

Just as it is with oneself, so it is with the deity, so with the fire, so with the jar, and so with the disciple; that very same rite—whether with parts (sakala), without parts (niṣkala), or supreme (parā)—must be performed in its entirety.
The one with form (sākāra) is said to possess all [attributes], bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
the formless (niṣkala), joined with Śakti, is the intermediate leader of mantras.
But that which terminates in Paraśakti is established as the essence of the Praṇava.
The manifest (vyakta), presided over by the Sakala [aspect], is of the nature of Prakṛti and has Viṣṇu as its form;
the unmanifest (avyakta), presided over by the Niṣkala [aspect], is to be known as proclaimed by Puruṣa. 10.
Everything—whether manifest or unmanifest—is of the nature of consciousness and is presided over by the Supreme Deity, who exists in the form of mantra and embodies both being and non-being;
he who knows this through the state of oneness is the liberator from saṃsāra. || 11 ||
The first [initiation] is for those who know the ritual; the second is for the practitioners themselves;
the third is always for those intent on liberation and for those in office; and the [fourth] must be performed for the teachers, bestowing union with Brahman. 12.
One should place the supreme mantra-maṇḍala within the womb of the fire;
one should offer oblations with all the mantras, preceded by Viṣṇu, ending with the word "svāhā. || 13 ||
For the divine limbs are the mantras; one should perform their satiation with sesame seeds and clarified butter according to one's ability, following the rule of ten parts for the mantras.
Thereafter, one should perform the initiation rite for the disciples as prescribed;
for each mantra, five oblations should be offered in succession. 15.
Thus, one becomes qualified for the worship of the scriptures before the divine fire;
thereafter, one should again perform a hundred oblations (homa) with the root mantra.
One should offer eighteen oblations with ghee alone or with sesame seeds as desired,
along with twenty-five for the goddesses and ten for the limbs.
One should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with clarified butter alone using the root mantra;
from that, there shall be initiation for men and for the practitioner's sake, for the purpose of attaining perfection. 18.
For disciples who desire liberation, one should gradually purify the path;
having meditated upon the fire as being like space, [one should contemplate] the sequence of the principles (tattva-paddhati) within its midst.
The instructor, having meditated, should join [the disciple] to each principle (tattva) in succession;
first, the seven primordial natures (prakṛti) are to be purified, and immediately after that, the Pradhāna.
Then, having purified the twenty-sixth [tattva], one should lead it to dissolution right there;
the forms of the subtle elements of sound and the rest [should be dissolved] by means of the heart and the other [centers] in due order. (21)
Therefore, one should purify the ego with the Astra-mantra, the intellect with the Jīva-mantra,
and the primary matter (pradhāna) with the middle mantra and the heart-mantras of the goddesses.
One should perform the twenty-sixth [syllable] with the Praṇava alone, and by that same [Praṇava], the conjunction;
first the birth through the Tattva, and thereafter again the sovereignty of the Tattvas. || 23 ||
Upon the completion of the fire-offering (homa) of the principles, there occurs the separation from other states of existence;
thereafter, the extraction (uddhāra) must be performed, principle by principle, in due order.
In this way, one should contemplate the fivefold action within each principle (tattva);
for there is nothing higher than the twenty-sixth, since having extracted [the soul], one would cast it back again. 25.
The child should always be laid down right there with the syllable Om (praṇava),
after having meditated upon the stainless Lord Viṣṇu, the all-pervading soul of the universe.
Having meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning or end, the infallible one whose form has transcended all change, [one should recite] the root mantra in reverse order.
One should employ the ritual of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) ending with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*;
having offered one hundred oblations for each principle (*tattva*) according to its own name.
The deity, joined with the mantra, should perform the fire-oblation for the nine principles:
Puruṣa in the first principle and Satya in the second.
One should join Acyuta with the third principle, Vāsudeva with the fourth, Pradyumna with the fifth principle, and the Great Lord with the sixth. 30.
Then Aniruddha, the large-eyed one, and after him Saṃkarṣaṇa;
he should be joined to the seventh principle (tattva), and likewise the goddesses should be joined to the eighth.
But in the ninth, the supreme reality, having meditated upon the all-pervading Nārāyaṇa, one becomes powerful,
possessed of great energy, virtuous in conduct, steadfast, and endowed with all excellent qualities.
One should take up residence in meritorious fields, at excellent holy fords, at the confluences of rivers,
and in places frequented by gods and sages.
Endowed with pure food and avoiding all forms of impurity,
the wise one should always recite the mantra three hundred thousand times, with his mind fully absorbed in the mantra.
By means of this, rites are accomplished; one may achieve subjugation and attraction, and the crushing of planetary afflictions, fevers, poisons, and malevolent spirits. (35)
Just as a hero who has encountered [the enemy] would properly employ the lord of mantras for the purpose of terrifying all the Śākinīs, so [should one act]. 36.
Having prepared a divine mandala, one should place a water-pot there;
having recited [the mantra] to the Lord Janārdana according to the previously mentioned procedure.
One should properly seat a pure man who is afflicted by disease upon a seat;
then, having consecrated flowers together with white mustard seeds, [one should perform the rite]. 38.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over them, he should, with both hands, visualize a triangular mandala marked by fire upon the patient's own hand. (39)
In the center of that, one should contemplate the Lord of the gods of gods, whose form is radiant energy, holding a blazing discus and mace in his hands, and threatening all the wicked. 40.
One should show that hand to the person to be subdued; it quickly causes possession.
Upon seeing it, all beings, afflicted by fear, enter into a state of possession.
Upon seeing that they have just entered, one should perform the binding of the topknot (śikhābandha) with the root mantra ending in "namaḥ" and encapsulated by the word "Indra. 42.
One should perform the binding of the directions there with ashes while holding the weapon-mantra in hand;
the wise one should strike [the area] with ashes consecrated by the recitation of the weapon-mantra. 43.
Furthermore, being enraged, one should strike [the enemy] with white mustard seeds over which the mantra has been recited seven times;
or one should strike them with creepers or reed-sticks over which the mantra has likewise been recited seven times.
One should offer guggulu incense, recited three times, to the patient;
then, having formed the Jayā-mudrā, one should recite the mantra eighty thousand times.
One should fashion its body as desired by means of this mantra;
one should strike it on the head with a mace and contemplate the conch-shell on the ear. 47.
Alternatively, one should fashion an image of the house out of cow dung;
if he does not release [the victim] quickly, one should cut his limbs with a discus. 48.
When he says, "I release [you]," then one should cause him to take an oath;
having offered the oblation, one should dismiss him and release the binding of the crest-lock (śikhā) and the directions.
One should meditate upon the mantra situated within the belly of the single letter (ekāra), conjoined with the sixteen digits (kalās), flowing as nectar, and resembling the orb of the moon. 50.
Having thus visualized the left hand, one should place it upon the head of the person to be treated;
having filled the body of the afflicted one with that nectar, one who is engaged in this rite shall remove poisons and demonic possessions. 51.
One should cause flowers, anointed with fragrant substances and consecrated seven times with mantras, to be placed in the left hand of women and in the right hand of men. 52.
By the power of the sovereign mantra, one immediately comes under its control;
having meditated upon the mantra, which resembles the orb of the moon, within the hollow of the hand. (53)
To whomsoever one shows that hand, one shall quickly bring them under control.
Having performed the previously mentioned nyāsa, one should meditate upon the form of Kāntā.
Standing before one who is angry, one should quickly bring that person under one's control;
furthermore, whatever leaf, flower, or fruit is given to someone after being consecrated with the mantra three times [achieves the same].
He quickly comes under control through the power of the Lord of Mantras.
Having meditated upon the three-deity Lord of the World with the three-syllabled mantra,
[one should regard] the disciple as having form (sakala) and likewise oneself as being without form (niṣkala).
Having likewise meditated upon the disciple, oneself, and the supreme [deity], one should cast [the disciple] into the supreme [state]. || 56 ||
At the end of the hundred [oblations], one should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the word "vauṣaṭ";
[it is] immeasurable, indescribable, incomparable, and free from disease.
Having offered the ten oblations, they become subtle, all-pervading, eternal, stable, imperishable, and sovereign; likewise, one should again offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having again meditated upon that which ends with *vauṣaṭ*, one should contemplate the triad as one:
the disciple, oneself, and the all-pervading, omnipresent Viṣṇu. (59)

Then, at the conclusion of the ritual procedure, having meditated upon that which has attained equanimity in one place, the initiation of Viṣṇu bestows liberation and grants freedom from the fear of worldly vision. 60.
When the lower reality passes into the higher reality, he should then unite the disciple with the Self, having performed the completion oblation according to the proper ritual procedure.
And having brought the disciple from there, one should unite him with the body of the disciple;
in this way, the initiation that bestows union with Viṣṇu is completed.
At the conclusion of the initiation, the Guru should perform the auspicious avabhṛtha bath;
likewise, the consecration (abhiṣeka) should be performed for the teacher and for those who are practitioners.
Likewise, at that time during the avabhṛtha rite, one should prepare a pitcher for the purpose of bathing;
indeed, with an auspicious pitcher that embodies all sacred fords (tīrthas). 64.
Having bathed, he should thereafter worship his guru and his attendants;
at the conclusion of the initiation, he should offer himself to the guru.
A village or a heap of jewels, or gold respectively;
as well as elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, along with groups of male and female slaves.
Whatever object is appropriate, or whatever by which the Guru is pleased—even if all such things are given—there would still be no discharge of debt toward the Guru.
[Only one] endowed with pure devotion, possessed of faith, and having conquered the senses [is free from debt]. 67.

At the time of initiation, however, the Guru must know the sequence of the principles (tattvas), both in their nature as objects of knowledge and as the state of practice, so that compassion may arise. 68.
By means of the purified subtle elements (tanmātras), beginning with the subtle element of smell and proceeding in sequence, these [gross elements]—
earth and the others, ending with space— become completely purified.
Within those [twenty-three principles], two groups consisting of the organs should be known:

first that consisting of the organs of action, and then that consisting of the organs of cognition. Thus, through the purification of the subtle elements (tanmātras), the twenty principles become pure.
By the purification of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the purification of the mind (manas) is said to occur here;
by the purified intellect (buddhi), the cognitions (pratyaya), including those involving error, become purified. (71)
By means of the pure Pradhāna, the manifest and unmanifest are purified;
and by means of the pure Twenty-sixth principle, the conscious Puruṣa is likewise purified.
That which is impure cannot be purified within the supreme reality; therein one should attain the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya).
One should effect dissolution right there, in that which has the nature of the Supreme Brahman.
Thus ends the chapter on initiation in the Jayottara. ||0||
Nārada said:
You have described the path of liberation and the ritual of initiation in due order;
now, please tell me correctly about the path of worldly enjoyment.
The Blessed One said:
Listen to the divine rites of the wise King of Mantras;
I shall explain them in brief for the purpose of accomplishing the rite of "Rising from the Netherworld" (pātālottiṣṭha). 2.
The practitioner, having become self-restrained and devoted to the observances of the mantra, should perform the preparation of the cloth, sword, collyrium, space, pill, and so forth. || 3 ||
If one should enter the royal court after consecrating and applying a sectarian mark (tilaka) made with yellow pigment, saffron, ashes, or sandalwood paste; 4.
One shall obtain great honor by the mere sight [of this]; there is no doubt in this matter.
This has been stated in brief as the fruit of the previously mentioned recitation. || 5 ||
Even actions not explicitly mentioned are swiftly accomplished when one is thus engaged;
indeed, through the previously described recitation characterized by the three qualities, one shall attain the perfection of Vaiyati.
Having reached the entrance of the cave, one should smear the sacrificial ground;
then, having worshipped with the mantra according to the rule, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed procedure.
Furthermore, [one may offer] with oil mixed with ghee, or with "buffalo-eyebrow" (mahiṣākṣa) resin,
or with fuel-sticks of milk-tree wood, or even with stalks of dūrvā grass.
When one hundred thousand oblations have been offered, one attains the perfection of Vaivari;
having pierced through all obstacles, one enters the supreme opening.
Having drunk this divine elixir, one shall possess the strength of Nārāyaṇa;
joined by young maidens, he shall sport until the dissolution of the earth.
On a level and pure patch of ground, treated with yellow pigment and saffron,
one should draw a clearly defined and beautiful sword measuring thirty finger-breadths, complete with its parts.
Having worshipped Janārdana there according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should,
with a concentrated mind, place the hand in the position of a fist and mutter [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
When the sword rises up, one should then seize it with the fist;
having grasped it, one shall become the sovereign of all the Siddhas.
One shall attain the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin) over all the vidyādharas;
one should worship the Lord of Mantras according to the previously mentioned procedure.

Having taken yellow pigment (rocanā) from a conch-shell or a pearl-oyster with the conch-gesture (śaṅkhamudrā), the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra as many times as it takes for it to emit flames. 15.
In their midst, a beautiful maiden in the form of a young girl will be seen;
she will say, "I am a Siddha," and she shall accomplish whatever task is desired. || 16 ||

By this very procedure, one should accomplish the preparation of collyrium and other substances, as well as yellow pigment (rocanā), saffron (kuṅkuma), yellow arsenic (haratāla), and realgar (manaḥśilā). || 17 ||
There, one should employ the *cakrāṅka* herb as the fifth;
having ground it finely, one should stir it with the three sweet substances.
Having worshipped the Lord of Mantras in the mandala on the eleventh day,
one should consecrate that pill within a leaf-casket.
Then, on the twelfth lunar day, one should worship according to the ritual procedure for the white Arka plant;
the practitioner of mantras should then recite it ten lakhs of times, and then it shall become perfected.
Holding her in his hand, the practitioner may roam within the expanse of the sky,
or in the netherworld, or upon the surface of the earth, or even in the cities of the world-protectors.
Just as Viṣṇu with the discus in hand is invisible to all the deities, so too does the lord of practitioners become [invisible] through the power of this mantra. || 22 ||
One should bring the corpse of either a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya that is free from wounds;
having placed it in an empty house, one should then bathe and worship it.
Having worshipped the mantra in the maṇḍala according to the prescribed ritual, the practitioner should place a corpse seated there and recite the mantra before it. 24.
One should strike it with one hundred and eight mustard seeds;
then, rising up with speed, it speaks these words while bowing down: || 25 ||
"I am your servant today; let my command be given to me—whether it be the foot-ointment, the elixir, or even the perfected alchemical potion. (26)
Whatever else is desired by the mind, one should also arrange that from among those [materials];
having brought silken cloth, one should have the Yakṣiṇī painted upon it.
Adorned with all ornaments, beautiful, and desired by the mind—the practitioner of mantras, having worshipped the mantra according to the prescribed rules as before, [should proceed]. 28.
Having observed the fast, one should offer guggulu incense at midnight;
one should perform this for seven days and always recite the mantra ten thousand times.
For at the seventh watch, at midnight, the cloth shakes audibly;
when the practitioner is no longer agitated, then it becomes perfected.
Whether she be a mother, a sister, or a wife, one should speak to her today with a mind free from doubt, saying whatever is desired; she,
being perfected, quickly fulfills all the desires of the practitioner.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the Chapter on Attainments, in the Jayottara.
Then, for the sake of the manifestation of yoga, one should practice the Vaiṣṇava yoga in a well-concealed, solitary place, free from dualities and possessing auspicious characteristics. || 1 ||
Having subdued pride and established his mind in the welfare of all beings,
he was devoted to the gods, the sacred fires, and his gurus, and was always intent upon the study of the true scriptures.
Abandoning malice toward living beings, untainted, with senses restrained,
he sat upon a most beautiful seat endowed with auspicious marks.
It should be fashioned from auspicious wood, measuring twenty-four finger-breadths in length,
with a well-proportioned height of twelve finger-breadths.
It was covered by someone with a well-washed garment placed over a black antelope skin,
or else with soft kuśa grass or some other material.

Seated there, he should constantly practice the limbs of yoga by means of the four [breath-control techniques], beginning with exhalation (recaka), distinguished by their respective measures (mātrās).
The minor, the middling, and the superior prāṇāyāma have been proclaimed;
thereafter one should perform pratyāhāra, and then the restraint of the mind (cittasaṃyamana).
Intellect (buddhi), mind (manas), and ego (ahaṅkāra)—these three are proclaimed as the consciousness (citta).
Nevertheless, one should diligently practice the withdrawal of the mind (pratyāhāra). 8.
The mind is said to be of four kinds; when joined with pratyāhāra (withdrawal), it remains fixed upon the path of the objective, but never otherwise. 9.
The mind is indeed fourfold; hear from me that in its entirety:
it is attached, well-absorbed, distracted, and characterized by coming and going. (10)
Dhyāna is proclaimed to be the accomplishment of the object of focus and the contemplation thereof;
from that, dhāraṇā is to be maintained, which is the unsurpassed attainment of the cool [state].
And that [recitation] is to be maintained in four ways according to the arrangement of each specific tantra;
while reciting, one should make the mantra expressive with eyes closed.

For the sake of understanding that which is to be expressed, one should perform it in three ways— consisting of the physical form (piṇḍa), the seed-syllable (bīja), and the word (pada)— namely, as whispered (upāṃśu), spoken aloud (vācya), and mental (mānasa).
Yoga is also said to be threefold, and it arises from the power of meditation:
the natural (prākṛta), the human (pauruṣa), and the third is the divine (aiśvarya). || 14 ||
Reasoning (tarka) is said to reside in the *ūha* [stage], and it investigates the means of attainment (*siddhi*).
But concentration (samādhi) is proclaimed as bliss (ānanda), which is the attainment of one's own self. || 15 ||
But when that Brahman, devoid of the utterance of mantras and free from parts, portions, and the like, manifests itself by abandoning the object of perception; || 16 ||
When meditative absorption (samādhi) is fully perfected, one attains the supreme human goal.
This practice is proclaimed to extend from the beginning of breath control (prāṇāyāma) up to the end of samādhi;
it is established through a distinction of measures (mātrā) that are doubled and tripled.
One should perform the yogic postures according to this procedure as it has been described.
One should bind the four yogic postures with a yogic belt. || 18 ||
Assuming one of these— either the paryaṅka, the acala, the bhadra, or the firm svastika posture— and keeping the body straight, he should proceed in due order.
With well-formed limbs and joints, he should possess broad chest and neck.
Having made the arms relaxed, one should slightly bend the head.
The two hands are positioned like tortoises at the navel and the middle of the hips.
Or else, the left hand should be placed upon the right, or the right hand upon the left.
Having turned the hands palm-upward, one should join the hands in the tortoise (kacchapya) position.
One should hold the neck with effort, neither too rigid nor bent. || 22 ||
Slightly closing the eyes while gazing at the tip of the nose,
one should cover the mouth as if with a lid and not let the teeth touch the teeth.
One should practice yoga with the internal seed (sagarbha) or without the internal seed (nirgarbha), remaining well-restrained.
Then, one should impel the wind known as prāṇa, conjoined with the mind.
Prāṇāyāma is proclaimed to have four divisions, beginning with recaka;
one should always strive with effort to conquer the mind, which is difficult even for gods and dānavas to subdue. 25.
Even if the mind is restrained by force through practice and dispassion,
one should nevertheless exert effort in the avoidance of limiting adjuncts.
These are to be known as twofold: those that are proximate and those arising from the mind.
They are closely associated, they are the very essence of strength, they arise from the mind, and they are fashioned by the mind.
But in a place not infested by gadflies and mosquitoes, motionless and free from odors,
he should remain with eyes closed, his faculty of taste fully restrained.

Thus, remaining firmly established in the true object of perception, one should completely abandon all adjuncts born of proximity as well as the various [impurities] arising from latent impressions. 29.
One should always withdraw the mind when it is distracted among all objects;
that mind which is thus withdrawn everywhere and at all times should be known as characterized by tamas.
From that, one should know the coming and going [of the mind] due to practice; that is the rajasic state.
The sattvic state is said to be when the mind is firmly attached to the range of the objective. 31.
Then, O ascetic, he should be known as "withdrawn" (saṃlīna), having transcended the qualities (guṇas);
he should thus perform meditation while the vital breath is restrained within the "pregnant" (sagarbha) state.
And it is further said that there are three kinds [of worship] beneficial for yogis:
the Sakala (with parts), the Niṣkala (without parts), and Viṣṇu as the third, who possesses the supreme form.

But the other [elements] should be known as threefold; one should contemplate the sound of space (ākāśa) as formless, while that of the God of gods as having form and possessing a perceptible appearance. 34.
Thus has meditation been fully described, until one becomes as pervasive as the limits of space;
for so long should one cultivate the focal point, until no focal point remains to be cultivated.
For one should perceive existence as having reached non-existence, and existence as the supreme state;
first one should practice the gross, then the subtle, and after that the supreme.
In this way, the mind dissolves along with the target and the meditative supports;
one should meditate upon the form of the God of gods within the sphere of the heart-lotus.
Then one should contemplate another object of focus, whether gross or otherwise subtle;
as he practices in this manner, an excellence of qualities arises for him. (38)
Then, piercing that which is even more subtle than that, one should know the next sound; having ascended above all mantras, it remains there.
Then, one should gradually contemplate [the seed-syllable] the size of a mustard seed,
which is the source produced by one's own power, at the end of which the Nāda is established.
That [wind], having arisen from that [void] and being as subtle as a horse's hair, always moves through the sky and enters the heart like the mind. 41.
Then one should contemplate the subtle [channel] the size of a hair on the head;
by practicing meditation with this, the Brahma-nāḍī is quickly perceived. 42.
Then, having established the restraint, one should meditate upon that which is the size of a single body hair, as fine as a lotus fiber, and which illuminates the Brahma-nāḍī. 43.
When that channel is seen, its face being devoid of resemblance, one should go to the supreme state by way of the path of the Brahmarandhra through it. 44.
Having thus meditated upon the partless [reality], he too becomes dissolved in the supreme state;
however, for one who contemplates that supreme state, the condition of *unmanatva* (transcendence of mind) arises.
Then, however, one's own existence, which has the nature of Brahman, becomes manifest;
or else, one should meditate upon the Lord, who is both with parts and without parts, in the form of sound. 46.
One should meditate upon the mantra consisting of Nārāyaṇa, beginning with the syllable Om (praṇava) and ending with the word "namas";
for this entire Supreme Lord is composed of sound. 47.
One should contemplate the single, partless syllable as *hūṃ*, *kṣāṃ*, or *hrīṃ*;
then, one should contemplate that partless drop (*bindu*) residing in the heart, which contains the three deities.
Then, although that power (śakti) has arisen, it is measured by the half-mātṛkā; that power dissolves into the nāda, and the nāda goes to dissolution in the Supreme (para). 49.
For in this way, through the yoga of meditation, they behold the supreme, eternal [reality];
or else, having expanded upon the *bindu* and *nāda*, one should contemplate them. 50.
Having dissolved of its own accord right there, it is right there that the supreme state resides;
or else, one should meditate upon that eternal reality which has the nature of space. 51.
One should always contemplate the sky of consciousness (cidvyoma), which abides both externally and internally and transcends the crest-lock (śikhātīta).
Having meditated upon this supreme state for the sake of liberation, one shall no longer be subject to worldly existence. 52.
Having meditated thus, liberation shall be attained; yet enjoyment remains established in the Sakala form—the body of the God of gods in the form of Viṣṇu. || 53 ||
The god who holds a conch and a lotus, adorned with a mace, a discus, and other weapons, four-armed, four-formed, four-faced, and possessed of beautiful eyes. 54.

One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, the best of gods, Kṛṣṇa, the victorious Hari, who is the subduer of all planets, seated upon the bird [Garuḍa], whose chest is adorned by Lakṣmī, and who is embellished with every kind of jewel.
The all-pervading Lord Hayagrīva, who assumes the form of Hari, brandishes his weapon;
and the Nārasiṃha form is shown to manifest both auspiciousness and inauspiciousness in one place.
By whom, having assumed a fierce form, the body of Kapila was sustained;
by whom, in his universal form, the bodies of the gods were always sustained.
O Saṃkarṣaṇa, O Viśālārka, O Pradyumna whose weapon is the flower,
and O omniscient Aniruddha— you alone are the Lord of the universe.
Just as the three Vedas were created by you as Brahman,
so too does Acyuta protect the virtuous in the three worlds for the sake of their preservation.
O Govinda, in your fierce form you destroy the world in an instant;
O Lord, in the form of the sacrifice, you receive the oblation of the gods through the mouth of Agni.
O Janārdana, you indeed receive the *kavya* offerings for the ancestors;
therefore, with devotion, I worship Hari, who bestows liberation from worldly existence.
Dāmodara in the form of a serpent, Vārāha the upholder of the earth,
Vāmana of concealed form, and Trivikrama of expansive limbs.
The Fish with its limbs withdrawn, and the Tortoise who upholds the world;
The god who brings about the happiness of the gods and bestows nectar upon the deities.
The god who brings an end to the Dānavas, manifesting in a female form,
upon whom rest all the worlds together with the oceans and seas.
Together with the gods and the dānavas, with the sages whose wealth is asceticism,
with men and the lords of men, and with the rivers along with the mountains.
In whose belly all things abide, and in whom all things at their end abide—you are the primordial source of this world; by meditating upon you, we have attained happiness. 66.
May we, together with our kinsmen, be free from fear in this world and the next by means of the divine *praṇava* consisting of three measures: *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*. 67.
O Lord, by means of your charming name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and likewise through the three Rāmas,
you have made a promise in the form of a swan through your illusory power (māyā).
I am the deliverer and you indeed are [the other]; we three are the saviors of the world.
I am the deliverer for you from the vast ocean of worldly existence.
Therefore, having come here quickly and entered, deliver yourself swiftly;
once entered, become the bestower of all perfections (*siddhis*) and prosperities (*bhūtis*).
When meditated upon in this manner, it shall then become the granter of success.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Yogapaṭala, in the Jayottara.
The Blessed One said:
Then one should consecrate the disciple, who is endowed with all auspicious marks, perfectly tranquil, clear-minded, self-controlled, and a worshiper of the gods. (1)
The consecration should be performed by the Guru for one who is devoted to the teacher, has conquered the senses, and abides by the time-periods prescribed in the scriptures;
for such a person, the consecration is to be performed by the Guru. || 2 ||
One should perform all the offices for the gurus, consisting of garlands and so forth;
the teacher, who knows the reality and is a knower of the yoga of knowledge, [presides] over all castes. || 3 ||
One should appoint a practitioner who is equal to the teacher in his qualities;
for one who abides by the ritual rules of the mantra-tattva, the consecration must be performed. 4.
He should not perform acts of harming or favoring in any rite whatsoever;
nor should he employ a mantra or a mudrā without the observance of the pledges (samaya).
Even while performing one's own practice, one should conceal every mantra by that very means; this protection of the mantra must be observed by him for the sake of attaining success in the mantra. 6.
Then, another [form of] constant enjoyment should always be understood by the Guru;
the third, the initiation into the principles (tattvābhiṣeka), should be given to one who desires liberation. || 7 ||
Having meditated upon the entire ladder of reality—both with parts and partless, supreme—and having honored them mentally or even with white, auspicious flowers; || 8 ||
However, for one who has undergone refinement, an auspicious consecration according to reality must be performed;
the consecration of the Guru is traditionally prescribed by means of the royal ritual of honor.
One who knows the three principles (tritattva) may initiate those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes in the reverse order; however, he should initiate all castes in the natural (direct) order.
One should prepare eight jars fashioned after the eight oceans,
well-filled with all kinds of jewels and endowed with all medicinal herbs.
Filled with all kinds of seeds and adorned with plantain leaves,
such were the jars established by the givers of truth.
One should worship all of this, or even just one of these, in a single vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, provided it possesses the required qualities.
It was well-adorned with fruits and roots, as well as sandalwood and other fragrant substances;
it was beautified by auspicious symbols such as the conch, the swastika, and the lotus, and graced by the svastika design.

When [the image] has a fine cloth tied around its neck or is covered with various garments, and when it is filled with water from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), one should worship the Lord of Mantras there. || 15 ||

First, one should worship [the deity] in the water-pot; then, that which resides in the center of the mandala; then, that which is situated in the fire; and thereafter, once again, within the body of the disciple.

Having further worshipped the deity residing in the preceptor immediately thereafter, one should then worship [the deity] in all the jars and other vessels with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in due order. || 17 ||
Having worshipped the Lord Mantreśvara according to the procedure previously described,
one should then worship the water-pot (kalaśa) there with the assembly of mantras and mudrās.
Having recited it one thousand and eight times correctly, one should meditate [on the vessel] as being completely filled with nectar and endowed with jewels and medicinal herbs. 19.
By this procedure, one should perform the consecration of the preceptor;
having placed upon his head an auspicious jar consecrated with mantras. (20)
Then, the office of authority should be granted, as well as volumes of the Saṃhitās;
and likewise an umbrella, a turban, a crown, sandals, and a seat.
Having placed [the image] upon the pedestal, the consecration of all [the deities] should be bestowed;
[this is done] upon a well-constructed two-cubit yogapīṭha that is eight times as high [as it is wide].
It was covered with a canopy, hung with garlands of flowers,
transformed into a seat for the mantra, and beautified by a scattering of parched grain.
One should draw an auspicious lotus or a svastika as a seat there;
having placed the disciple upon it, one should practice the mantra.
Then the practitioner, or even the teacher, should consecrate the disciple;
or a king seeking victory, or even one of poor fortune seeking good fortune. (25)
A woman desiring a son, a maiden seeking a husband,
or anyone who desires long life should bathe there every year.
The wise man should bathe according to his means amidst various musical sounds accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas; having bathed, he should worship his guru.
And with various collections of goods accompanied by attendants, as well as with diverse jewels, villages, horses, cattle, and so forth. || 28 ||
With various kinds of wealth and with devotion—by whatever means the Guru is satisfied—one should perform this rite every year according to this rule. (29)
Indeed, bathing performed without hesitation leads to the destruction of death;
for as many years as one performs it, one remains free from disease, liberated from wrinkles and grey hair, fortunate, and possessed of stable youth. (30)
When the time for battle has arrived, one should consecrate the weapons with mantras;
having performed the previously mentioned nyāsa and consecrated them according to the proper rite, one should cast [the weapon] into the midst of the army, which will destroy the enemy soldiers. 31.

One should write [the name] combined with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma), interspersed with the name-mantra, within the interior of the letter E, endowed with the sixteen digits (kalās). 32.
Outside of that, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with a pericarp;
just as the goddesses and their limbs are arranged in the worship, so should one depict them upon the petals.
It shall paralyze all divine weapons and destroy the Khārkhoda missiles. Written on birch bark and placed within a jar of milk,
it shall destroy even the most violent portents accompanied by malevolent sorcery.
Whoever always wears [this] on the arm, the neck, or likewise on the head,
for him no fear arises from poison, disease, fire, or elemental spirits.
O twice-born one, this procedure for the mantra, along with the fruits of its ritual placement (nyāsa), has been described by me for the rites of consecration,
as well as for those of pacification and nourishment.
For the sake of protection from all beings, it should be employed everywhere and at all times;
and this king of mantras, once accomplished, brings about all spiritual attainments.
Whatever rite exists on the surface of the earth that has not yet been accomplished, all of it quickly grants every desire through mere remembrance. || 38 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter, on consecration, in the Jayottara.
The Blessed One said: "O best of sages, O you whose wealth is austerity, I shall now declare another matter:
the power, the preeminence, and the sovereign majesty of this king of mantras. (1)
He by whom this has been properly worshipped, known, meditated upon, and remembered even once—
his perfection is supreme and divine, and he indeed dwells in heaven.
And no mantra equal to this king of mantras exists;
having recited this lord of mantras, one shall attain all desires. (3)
And there is no mantra equal to this, even by hundreds of millions of mantras;
having obtained this supreme mantra, cast away everything like straw.
Just as the wish-fulfilling gem in this world bestows whatever is desired,
even so does this best of men grant [all things] to the practitioner.
Before whichever deity one recites this Lord of Mantras, that deity,
being pleased, bestows upon him all his desires.
He who, for a full year, offers oblations of black-seeded sesame seeds numbering one hundred thousand, and at the conclusion offers oblations of clarified butter; ||| 7 ||
This Lord of Mantras swiftly bestows upon him eleven thousand vast riches, together with lotus-territories.
Villages, horses, gold, and whatever ornaments are made or unmade;
longevity, sons, as well as health, good fortune, and success in every direction—[may these be yours]. 9.
What need is there for much speaking here? By reciting the mantra while offering libations to the five Viṣṇus, one shall obtain all desires. || 10 ||

When one million or ten million recitations have been performed, the practitioner shall accomplish the powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā) by means of recitation alone, even without the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma). || 11 ||
"He beholds that god Viṣṇu in person, possessed of the supreme form.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, has this entire secret been recounted to you.
O observer of noble vows, it should not be given to one of evil character, nor to one devoted to cruel deeds, nor to one who approaches with deceit, nor to an atheist.
This scripture should be given to one who is devoted to the guru, self-controlled, intent on the service of the deity, and dedicated to the commands of the guru.
Without a guru, there is no attainment of the scriptures on this earth;
nor is there the attainment of purificatory rites, nor eligibility for the mantras. || 15 ||
Therefore, with every effort, devotion to the guru should always be practiced;
for the propitiation of the guru is the root of all proper conducts. 16.
Thus, O sage, this entire Jayottara has been narrated to you;
wherever this remains written, there prosperity prevails.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Jayottara.
Thus ends the Jayottara within the Jayākṣarasaṃhitā.
